title: Concord AI exit and serving parity check
next_steps: Redwood: send parity checklist + benchmark spreadsheet and pricing range (by 2025-02-18)
Concord: share sample prompt corpus and token distribution (by 2025-02-18)
Schedule POC kickoff for week of 2025-02-24
Security: share SOC 2 + network diagram + KMS integration notes
action_items: Rachel Kim - Send parity checklist, benchmark template, and pricing estimate - 2025-02-18
Miguel Santos - Draft expected performance baseline and suggested test prompts for Concord workloads - 2025-02-20
Priya Rao - Provide sample prompt corpus and token distribution stats - 2025-02-18
Jenna Hale - Share procurement timeline and SSO/SAML contact - 2025-02-17
summary: Initial discovery with Concord AI about moving serving from a vertex/open/hosted stack to Redwood. Focus on compatibility with existing models (TGI/vLLM exported checkpoints), eval parity concerns, latency/cost targets, and security (VPC/KMS/SOC2). AE/SE outlined Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private options, and proposed a POC to validate perf and quality parity. Concord requested parity checklist and benchmark template; Redwood to propose pricing and dedicated sizing.
topics: Deployment modes: hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC
Security: SOC2, KMS, SSO, audit logs
Performance targets: p50/p99 latency, batching, KV cache
transcript:
[00:00] Rachel Kim: hey everyone thanks for taking time today um we scheduled 50 minutes to run through where concord is at and what you need from a migration/exit standpoint, i'm rachel kim account exec for redwood.
[00:12] Priya Rao: hi rachel, thanks. i'm priya, cto at concord. we brought tom and marcus and jennah from procurement. we just want to understand tradeoffs and risk, especially around eval parity.
[00:22] Rachel Kim: totally, and miguel from our se team will cover technical depth — miguel?
[00:26] Miguel Santos: hey all, morning, yeah i'll try to hit perf and compatibility notes. quick question before i start — are you currently running models on vertex or self-hosted vLLM?
[00:36] Tom Park: so it's a mix. prod is on vertex ai with signed calls to openai-compatible api for a few models, and dev/benchmarks we run vLLM/TGI on our k8s. most of our fine-tune checkpoints are in HF format; tokenizer is byte-level bpe variants.
[00:52] Marcus Li: and infra-wise we have a private subnet but it's in gcp for now; procurement wants to avoid a hard vendor lock and also needs SOC2 controls.
[01:02] Rachel Kim: understood. high level: Redwood offers hosted api for fastest time-to-value, dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and a private deployment that sits in your vpc — same api surface. the POC we typically do can validate perf and eval parity across those modes.
[01:20] Priya Rao: can you explain how compatibility works? like, if we bring over vLLM/TGI exported checkpoints will they run straight away? or do we need to recompile/convert?
[01:28] Miguel Santos: good question. short answer: usually yes but there are caveats. we support loading HF checkpoints and a range of llm model families. sometimes tokenizers differ — we run a tokenizer parity step where we compare tokenization on a sample corpus. also some custom ops in vLLM or TGI wrappers require conversion; we have tooling to detect ops and map to our runtime kernels but complex custom kernels may need engineer time.
[01:52] Tom Park: hmm ok. tokenization parity is a big one for us — small changes in tokenization skew eval metrics. how do you ensure parity?
[02:00] Miguel Santos: we run a three stage check: tokenizer diff, logits-level check on a fixed prompt set, then ngram/likelihood comparisons across a corpus. if logits diverge beyond a threshold we surface a regression and root cause — could be tokenizer, quantization differences, or kernel precision.
[02:18] Priya Rao: do you support our current quantization profile? we use 4-bit q8+ from the vllm toolchain in some places.
[02:25] Miguel Santos: we have quantization-friendly execution paths; we can ingest quantized weights in certain formats or re-quantize during onboarding. depending on model family we recommend specific quant profiles — we'll flag which models are safe for 4-bit and which need 8-bit to preserve accuracy. we'll include recommended configs in the parity checklist.
[02:42] Marcus Li: latency is also huge. our SLO is 150ms p50 for single-turn completions at typical seq len of 128 and p99 under 600ms. can you meet that on hosted?
[02:52] Rachel Kim: for many of our smaller models yes on hosted; for consistent p99 at that latency we often recommend dedicated pools so you don't get noisy neighbor variability. dedicated also gives you reserved capacity and predictable queuing.
[03:05] Miguel Santos: also prefix and KV cache behavior matters for multi-turn chat. our runtime supports KV cache reuse and sharded caches across GPUs to reduce token compute; we'll simulate your traffic pattern during POC.
[03:17] Tom Park: right, we saw big differences when token reuse wasn't identical. how do you handle batching — we have peaks from background scoring jobs and spikes from product UI.
[03:25] Miguel Santos: Redwood does continuous batching with workload-aware heuristics; you can set latency SLOs and batching will adapt. for scoring pipelines we recommend separate dedicated routes or a dedicated pool with autoscale burst.
[03:36] Priya Rao: security: SOC2 is baseline. we also need KMS integration for keys and ability to rotate keys. private deployment must run inside our VPC and support customer-managed HSM ideally.
[03:47] Rachel Kim: we support KMS integrations (GCP/AWS) and bring-your-own-key workflows for private deployments. HSM integrations are available as part of our enterprise package. we'll include network diagram and KMS notes.
[03:58] Jenna Hale: procurement question: if we go dedicated, what are typical commit terms and exit clauses? we have to present a vendor risk plan.
[04:06] Rachel Kim: typical reserved capacity contracts are monthly or annual; we can do trial credits and short pilot commitments. exit clauses — we'll provide language around data deletion, model artifacts, and portability — we aim to avoid lock-in, and we'll support exporting your model checkpoints and metadata.
[04:20] Marcus Li: exporting metadata and exact runtime config is key. we don't want silent differences in kernels to change model behavior.
[04:27] Miguel Santos: agreed — we'll produce a reproducible ship of the POC including kernel flags, quant settings, tokenizer config, and a regression test report. that way you can see line-by-line where diffs arise.
[04:39] Priya Rao: excellent. about evals: our product owners want no more than 5% regression on our primary metrics when we switch. how do you measure and triage?
[04:49] Miguel Santos: we'll take your metric list, run an A/B on your prompt suite of maybe 5–10k prompts (you can provide representative sample), and compute delta on log-likelihood, ROUGE-like scores, and custom task metrics. if we see regression beyond agreed thresholds, we do root cause analysis — tokenizer, quant, or kernel numeric stability — and propose mitigations: different quant profile, small fine-tune, or run on higher precision.
[05:10] Tom Park: small fine-tune? would you support a quick distilled tune to fix distribution shift?
[05:14] Miguel Santos: yes we offer options: local fine-tune guidance, or you can run a lightweight calibration with a small dataset. some customers accept a small 5–10k-steps calibration to align logits.
[05:26] Rachel Kim: quick interjection — pricing. performance and cost tradeoffs: hosted is pay-as-you-go, dedicated has committed monthly spend and lower per-token unit cost. private has platform fees plus infra. we'll give a ballpark today and a detailed estimate in the follow-up.
[05:40] Jenna Hale: ballpark now would help us decide if dedicated is realistic.
[05:44] Rachel Kim: sure — for a pool sized for your expected 8k qps token-hours we'd estimate X — sorry i don't have the exact number in my head, we'll send an initial range in the follow-up.
[05:55] Priya Rao: ok. another technical point: we sometimes use custom TGI server plugins; will that break if we move?
[06:02] Miguel Santos: custom TGI plugins can be a blocker. we have a plugin compatibility checklist; if the plugin calls custom CUDA kernels it likely needs porting. if it's a python-level hook we can often wrap it. we'll run an ops scan in the POC.
[06:18] Tom Park: we also use chunked context windows and long-sequence attention tricks — does Redwood runtime support flash attention variants?
[06:24] Miguel Santos: our runtime selects kernels based on model architecture and hardware — it supports a range of optimized attention kernels including flash-attention-like implementations. we test against your sequence length distribution during perf tests.
[06:37] Priya Rao: regarding data residency — we need EU data for EU customers. can hosted be region-restricted?
[06:43] Rachel Kim: yes hosted supports region pins; for stricter controls private deployments inside your cloud or on-prem is recommended.
[06:50] Marcus Li: monitoring and observability: we need token-level cost breakdown and per-route latency. do you expose tracing?
[06:58] Miguel Santos: Redwood Console exposes per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost, and you can stream traces to your datadog or splunk. we also provide hooks for custom metrics.
[07:10] Tom Park: any known regressions when moving from vLLM to your runtime? we had one case where sampling randomness changed small response selection.
[07:18] Miguel Santos: sampling RNG seeds can differ; we can seed and make sampling deterministic for parity checks. crowdsourced randomness differences are expected but we control pseudo-rng and sampling algorithm parity for tests.
[07:30] Priya Rao: lifecycle ops: model rollouts, canary, A/B?
[07:34] Rachel Kim: yes we support canary deploys, A/B, automatic fallback policies — you can pin model versions and do staged rollouts with traffic splits.
[07:42] Jenna Hale: procurement again — legal: do you have standard DPA and data deletion commitments?
[07:47] Rachel Kim: yes we'll provide DPA, SOC2 attestation, and standard data retention options; private deployments give you full control.
[07:57] Priya Rao: if we go ahead with POC what's the timeline?
[08:00] Miguel Santos: typical POC is 2–4 weeks: week 1 onboarding and tokenizer/parity checks, week 2 perf tests and regression, week 3 mitigation and tuning, week 4 wrap and runbook. we can compress depending on sync frequency.
[08:14] Tom Park: do you have a benchmark sheet we can fill?
[08:18] Rachel Kim: yes we'll send one — it's the parity checklist + benchmark template. includes token distribution, prompt samples, seq lengths, and perf targets.
[08:26] Marcus Li: what's your support during POC? will we get an se dedicated?
[08:29] Rachel Kim: yes miguel will be primary se, alex will help on infra and onboarding.
[08:34] Miguel Santos: i'll run the perf harness and help configure the runtime and quant settings.
[08:38] Priya Rao: good. question about logs: we need audit logs of who queried what — is that available?
[08:44] Miguel Santos: yes audit logs are available with user-level metadata, redaction options, and retention policies per account.
[08:50] Tom Park: any limitations with openai-compatible API patterns? we use a couple of proprietary kwargs in our wrappers.
[08:56] Rachel Kim: Redwood API aims to be compatible but we do have some differences on extended params. we can map most wrappers; we'll document exact compatibility matrix.
[09:06] Priya Rao: what about embeddings and similarity search pipelines? we want consistent vector outputs.
[09:11] Miguel Santos: embeddings are part of the parity checks; small numeric differences can happen across float precision/quant, but we track nearest-neighbor stability and will propose reindexing if needed.
[09:23] Tom Park: cost sensitivity: we batch a lot of background jobs. do you support dedicated cheap scoring nodes?
[09:29] Rachel Kim: yes you can allocate lower-cost quantized nodes for scoring and higher-precision nodes for critical inference. that's a common hybrid pattern.
[09:37] Priya Rao: how do we handle secrets and keys in private deployment? we want KMS-backed keys with rotation schedules enforced by us.
[09:44] Miguel Santos: private control plane can integrate with your KMS; keys can be stored in cloud KMS or HSM, and rotation policies are configurable.
[09:50] Jenna Hale: quick note, procurement wants an initial cost range before our vendor shortlisting on 2025-02-20.
[09:56] Rachel Kim: we'll aim to get a preliminary estimate by 2025-02-18.
[10:00] Priya Rao: ok. small nit — does your runtime expose runtime flags for deterministic token logit dumps? we need reproducible logs for audits.
[10:09] Miguel Santos: yes we can dump logits and tokenization layers with config flags; for production we advise controlled dumps due to size.
[10:18] Tom Park: about model export — you said you support exporting artifacts, is it a binary blob or standardized HF format?
[10:24] Miguel Santos: we deliver an export package that includes HF-compatible checkpoints where possible plus a metadata manifest that records kernel flags, quant settings, and tokenizer.
[10:34] Rachel Kim: sounds like we're aligned on next steps. any blocker that would prevent a POC in the next two weeks?
[10:40] Priya Rao: procurement needs cost first but tech-wise no blocker. we'd need a short non-prod environment for tests.
[10:46] Marcus Li: network peering for private tests we can set up in a few days.
[10:50] Jenna Hale: procurement will send requirements doc and timeline.
[10:54] Rachel Kim: cool — recap: we'll send parity checklist + benchmark template, security pack, and a ballpark pricing/dedicated sizing by 2025-02-18. concord will share prompt corpus and token stats. schedule POC kickoff week of 2025-02-24. any other asks?
[11:13] Priya Rao: please include a short list of known vLLM/TGI compatibility caveats in the checklist.
[11:18] Miguel Santos: will do.
[11:20] Rachel Kim: thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email and set the calendar invite for kickoff.
[11:26] Tom Park: thanks, bye.
[11:27] meeting_end: 11:27
